Her face: porcelain skin with visible nose pores, natural asymmetry that the mirror reverses and subtly corrects, dark hair hiding one eye on the real side while the reflection shows both. Shot in Cronenweth's Blade Runner interior style — warm amber practicals mixed with cold blue-silver city light from the window, the mirror doubling and inverting the split. Kodak 5293 grain moderate, golden warm bias. Anamorphic breathing between subject and reflection. The palette is luxury-uncertain: champagne silk, amber, blue-silver, skin warmth, mirror chrome.

prompts.title: 60s — Creature Lagoon
prompts.subject: a young woman
prompts.text: A medium shot at water level — camera at the studio tank surface, water occasionally splashing the lens. A young woman treads water in a tropical lagoon set — practical palms with visible pot bases, a painted sky meeting the water line. Water dyed deep blue-green that Eastmancolor renders with vivid unnatural saturation. She wears a white swimsuit gone translucent in the water, hair floating in a dark halo. Her face tilted up catching the overhead arc light, expression between wonder and fear, water beading on her skin as tiny lenses. Beneath her — a dark indistinct mass moves. A practical rubber fin breaks the surface five meters behind, expanding ripples reaching her shoulders. Studio tank edges show at the far background, hidden by practical reeds. Shot on 70mm Eastmancolor — near-grainless, water's blue-green luminous, white swimsuit going slightly green from reflected color. The palette is creature-feature: tropical blue-green, white, dark water, warm skin, ominous dark shape.

prompts.title: 70s — Post-Nuke Highway
prompts.subject: a young man
prompts.text: A wide elevated shot — a devastated highway stretching to the horizon, cracked and buckled, abandoned rusting vehicles in both lanes, weeds through asphalt. A young man walks down the center line, small in the landscape, carrying a heavy pack and dragging a salvage-loaded travois. He wears a military field jacket with removed insignia leaving a darker rectangle, a hoodie underneath, leather gloves with worn-through fingertips, wire-reattached boot soles visible as metallic glint. His gait shows fatigue — favoring one leg. The highway: dust-opaque windshields, deflated cracked tires, an overturned school bus, bent road signs. Vegetation reclaims the roadside unnaturally. The sky shot through a tobacco-grad filter implying atmospheric contamination. Shot on Kodak 5254 — heavy documentary grain, tobacco filter combining with the stock's warm bias pushing everything into sepia-amber. Long lens compresses the highway into a dense hopeless queue. The palette is ash-warm: cracked asphalt, rust, faded military, tobacco sky, warm human skin point.

prompts.title: 80s — Alien Queen Chamber
prompts.subject: a young woman
prompts.text: A wide shot in Adrian Biddle's Aliens visual tradition — a vast organic chamber, walls and ceiling of practical resin castings suggesting biological architecture: ribbed glistening surfaces, hanging translucent tendrils dripping practical fluid, egg-shaped floor formations steaming from hidden dry ice. A young woman at the entrance, silhouetted against the chamber's amber practicals hidden within resin walls. She wears a loader-suit exoskeleton — metal tubing with hydraulic joints, bolted to boots and harness, the metal showing impact marks. Under the frame, a sweat-dark tank top, dog tags swinging, forearm tendons from gripping frame controls. Her face: controlled terror, jaw clenched, eyes scanning, the amber light catching a thin sweat line on her upper lip. The resin walls continuously misted with glycerin — viscous liquid catching every source in undulating highlights. Shot on Kodak 5293 — heavy grain, amber practicals pushing warm while the entrance stays cool blue-gray. Anamorphic breathing on organic curves. The palette is hive-interior: amber resin, wet translucent, industrial gray exoskeleton, warm sweating skin, cold blue escape.

prompts.title: 70s — Drive-In Saucer
prompts.subject: a young couple
prompts.text: A wide shot from inside a car looking out through the windshield at a drive-in screen showing a flying saucer film-within-film, washed out and flickering. On the bench seat, a young couple: he in a denim jacket with collar up, arm around her; she in a suede vest over floral blouse, head on his shoulder. They're not watching — her eyes closed, his looking at her. The dashboard: chrome bezels, a dangling air freshener, a paper drive-in ticket in the sun visor. Other cars visible in silhouette, windshields reflecting the saucer movie in miniature. A speaker hangs from the half-open window. Interior details: cracked vinyl seat, smudged rearview mirror, half-empty soda bottle. Their skin in projection wash is cool blue-white, but dashboard amber gauge lights add warmth — two temperatures simultaneously. Shot on Kodak 5254 for low-light — heavy grain giving home-movie intimacy. The palette is drive-in nocturnal: projection blue-white, dashboard amber, denim, suede, night black.

prompts.title: 80s — Last Star Fighter Arcade
prompts.subject: a young man
prompts.text: A medium shot in a darkened suburban arcade — light only from gaming cabinet screens, each projecting different colors onto surrounding surfaces. A young man at a cabinet seen from behind and slightly to the side, face lit by a vertical shooter's glow — pixel art reflected in wide eyes. He wears a members-only jacket in gray, collar popped, over a band graphic tee barely visible, acid-washed jeans, high-top sneakers. Body language: total absorption, shoulders hunched, one hand gripping a joystick worn smooth from a thousand players, the other hovering over the fire button. The arcade: rows of cabinets with painted plywood side art, silhouetted players, a dropped quarter on the carpet, a paper cup on a nearby cabinet. The carpet's specific commercial arcade pattern — geometric, dark, stain-hiding. Multiple screens create chromatic fog: orange, cyan, magenta overlapping on ceiling tiles and jacket. Shot on Kodak 5293 — grain extreme and dancing in near-black areas, each screen creating its own color island, CRT scan lines and screen curvature visible. The palette is arcade-chromatic: each screen its own world, darkness between them absolute, the human figure receiving all colors simultaneously.

prompts.title: 70s — Sentai Team Quarry Pose
prompts.subject: five figures
prompts.text: A wide shot on 16mm Fuji stock — the coarse, warm grain of Japanese television production circa 1975 — of five figures standing in a dramatic V-formation at the lip of a gravel quarry, each wearing a full-body spandex suit in a different primary color: red center, blue and yellow flanking, pink and green at the edges. The suits are visibly handmade — the spandex pulls at the crotch seams, the boots are clearly modified motorcycle boots spray-painted to match, and the helmets are fiberglass shells with tinted visors whose edges show the gel-coat finish and a visible seam line running from crown to chin. Each figure holds an identical pose: legs spread wide, one fist raised to the sky, the other arm crossed at the chest — the choreography precise but the physical effort visible in the trembling of held positions. The quarry behind them is undressed — no set dressing, just raw gravel slopes and exposed rock face, the production having relied entirely on the inherent drama of industrial excavation as alien landscape. A practical pyrotechnic charge has been detonated at the quarry floor — a column of orange smoke and gravel debris rises in the background, slightly off-center from the planned mark, one performer flinching almost imperceptibly from the blast. The 16mm stock renders the colors with the specific saturation profile of 70s Japanese television: reds bleeding slightly into orange, blues going slightly cyan, the yellow suit appearing almost chartreuse. Grain dances visibly across the entire frame. The lighting is pure exterior — harsh midday Japanese sun creating deep shadows under the helmets' chin guards, the quarry's pale gravel acting as a massive reflector that fills the shadows with warm bounce. Dust from the pyrotechnic hangs in the air, catching the sunlight. The palette is sentai-primary: red, blue, yellow, pink, green against quarry gray and pyrotechnic orange. The mood is the specific earnestness of 70s tokusatsu — five adults in spandex standing in a rock pit with absolute conviction that this is heroism.

prompts.title: 70s — Rubber Kaiju City Stomp
prompts.subject: a monster figure
prompts.text: A wide shot of a miniature city set — approximately 1:25 scale — being methodically destroyed by a performer in a rubber monster suit. The miniature buildings are balsa wood and plaster construction, some with hand-painted window details and tiny curtains visible through the clear plastic panes, electrical wiring running through the streets providing working streetlights that are currently flickering from the vibration of the monster's footsteps. The monster suit is a masterwork of foam latex and urethane: a bipedal reptilian creature with dorsal spines made of rigid fiberglass painted in metallic blue-green, the suit's chest showing compression wrinkles where the performer bends, the mouth mechanism operated by a cable visible at the neck when the head turns past 45 degrees, and small eye holes hidden in the creature's nostrils through which the performer's actual eyes occasionally catch the light. The monster's foot — an oversized rubber platform shoe — comes down on a three-story building whose walls collapse inward with satisfying practical destruction: the plaster crumbling, tiny furniture pieces scattering, a miniature car on the street below bouncing from the impact. Pyrotechnic squibs embedded in the building's base fire on cue, producing small orange fireballs that the 16mm Fuji stock renders with vivid, slightly orange-shifted warmth. The sky behind the miniature cityscape is a painted cyclorama in sunset tones — the brush strokes visible at the upper edge where the canvas curves. Wires suspending power lines between miniature poles are visible against the painted sky. Shot from a low angle to sell the scale — the camera positioned at "street level" within the miniature set, a few tiny model cars and lampposts in the foreground adding depth. The grain is heavy — 16mm pushed one stop for the interior stage lighting — and the color temperature shifts between the warm practicals in the miniature buildings and the cooler overhead studio lights illuminating the monster suit. The palette is destruction-warm: rubble gray, fire orange, monster blue-green, painted sunset. The mood is the pure, handcrafted joy of tokusatsu destruction — every building built by hand to be destroyed by foot, the monster's cable-operated jaw roaring silently in this frozen frame.

prompts.title: 80s — Bioman Helmet Close-Up
prompts.subject: a performer
prompts.text: An extreme close-up on a sentai helmet — the visor filling two-thirds of the frame, the camera so close that the fiberglass shell's texture is visible as a fine orange-peel surface beneath the glossy red paint, with a hairline crack at the temple from a stunt impact that's been filled with automotive body filler and repainted slightly off-shade. The tinted visor reflects the quarry landscape and the camera operator — a ghostly figure with a Bolex visible in the curved reflection. Behind the visor, barely perceptible: the performer's actual eyes, dark and focused, sweat beading on their brow, the foam padding of the helmet interior pressing against their forehead leaving a visible compression mark at the visor's upper edge. The helmet's chin guard shows wear marks from repeated donning — the paint rubbed to bare fiberglass at the pressure points. A tiny antenna on the helmet's crown — a chrome-plated car aerial repurposed — catches the sun in a hard flare. The neck seal where helmet meets suit shows a strip of black elastic fabric that doesn't quite match the red spandex of the suit, the junction held by hidden snaps whose outline is visible as small bumps under the fabric. Shot on 16mm with a macro adapter — the shallow depth of field at this distance isolates the visor in sharp focus while the helmet's crown and the background dissolve into soft bokeh. The 16mm grain is prominent at this magnification — each grain cluster visible as individual silver halide particles. The lighting is golden hour exterior — warm, directional, the visor acting as a curved mirror that compresses the entire world into a distorted panorama. The palette is hero-red: glossy paint, chrome antenna, tinted visor amber, the ghost of human eyes behind plastic. The mood is the intimate reality behind the spectacle — inside the helmet, it's just a person sweating.

prompts.title: 70s — Spectreman Giant Battle
prompts.subject: a giant hero figure
prompts.text: A wide shot on a miniature city set — a giant hero figure approximately 40 meters tall in the narrative, realized as a performer in a silver-and-blue bodysuit wrestling a rubber monster amid 1:40 scale buildings. The hero suit is smooth silver spandex with blue geometric panels sewn on — the stitching visible at the panel edges, the spandex stretched thin enough at the elbows and knees to show the performer's skin tone beneath. His helmet is a chrome-finished fiberglass piece with an oversized fin and a single red jewel on the forehead — the jewel is a plastic cabochon from a craft store, glued in place, catching the studio lights in a bright specular point. The monster he grapples with is a magnificent rubber disaster: a vaguely insectoid creature with mandibles made from painted foam that flex unconvincingly when the performer inside moves his jaw, compound eyes fashioned from ping-pong balls painted red and mounted in the foam latex head, and arms whose joint articulation is limited to the human performer's actual elbow and shoulder range inside the suit, creating that characteristic stiff-armed tokusatsu grapple. They wrestle amid miniature buildings — some already damaged from previous takes, walls cracked and leaning, tiny power lines dangling from their poles. The studio floor is visible at the miniature set's edges — painted gray concrete with gaffer tape marks. A practical smoke machine pumps theatrical haze between the buildings from a hidden tube. Shot on 16mm Fuji stock with the characteristic warm cast — the silver suit going slightly golden, the monster's red eyes oversaturating, the grain churning in the smoke. The lighting is flat overhead studio illumination supplemented by a single key from camera-right that creates dramatic shadows on the buildings but flattens the suit textures. The palette is battle-primary: silver, blue, red monster eyes, miniature city gray, smoke white. The mood is tokusatsu's essential contract — two people in rubber suits fighting between plywood buildings, and it's genuinely thrilling.

prompts.title: 80s — San Ku Kai Cockpit
prompts.subject: a young man
prompts.text: A medium shot inside a spacecraft cockpit set — the Japanese space-opera aesthetic of late-70s/early-80s tokusatsu, where Star Wars ambitions meet Toei studio budgets. A young man sits in a pilot's chair made from a modified barber's chair with fiberglass panels bolted to the armrests, the panels studded with illuminated buttons — the buttons are actual arcade cabinet components, their translucent caps glowing from incandescent bulbs behind them. He wears a silver flight suit with a standing collar and diagonal chest strap, the suit's polyester fabric catching the cockpit lights in a cheap, flat sheen, the zipper pull a standard YKK component visible at the collar. A helmet with a tinted visor rests on his knee — the visor scratched from use. His face shows genuine concentration — sweat at the temples from the hot studio lights, the makeup department's attempt at "space pallor" reading as a too-even foundation that stops at the jawline. Through the cockpit's viewport — a rear-projection screen showing a star field that's clearly a photograph of glitter scattered on black velvet, the individual glitter particles visible as tiny squares rather than points. The cockpit shakes — the camera operator physically rocking the tripod while two crew members push the cockpit set from opposite sides, the resulting motion slightly out of sync. Console lights flicker from a crew member manually toggling the power strip off-screen. Shot on 16mm — the grain heavy in the dark cockpit interior, the rear-projected starfield showing a different grain structure from the live-action foreground, the two stocks visibly mismatched. The palette is budget-space: silver polyester, arcade-button colors, glitter starfield, warm skin under too-even foundation. The mood is San Ku Kai's specific charm — ambition expressed through available materials, the cosmos realized with glitter and barber chairs, and the actor selling it completely.

prompts.title: 70s — Monster Transformation
prompts.subject: a performer
prompts.text: A sequence of three rapid shots composited into a single frame — the tokusatsu transformation effect achieved entirely in-camera. Left panel: a civilian figure — jeans, windbreaker — leaping into the air against a neutral sky, the wire harness visible as a thin dark line at the waist, the jump exaggerated by undercranking the camera to 18fps, making the movement unnaturally fast and floaty. Center panel: a burst of practical pyrotechnic flash — a magnesium charge fired at chest height, the overexposure blooming outward in a white starburst that eats into the surrounding frame, a few sparks visible as orange streaks trailing downward. Right panel: the transformed hero landing in a full sentai suit — red spandex, white boots, a helmet with an insect motif — in a low crouch with one fist touching the ground and the other arm swept back, the pose held with visible muscular tension. The wire from the jump is now hidden by the suit's belt, but the harness buckle produces a small bump under the spandex at the lower back. The three panels share the same quarry background — rocky slopes and scrub vegetation — but the lighting shifts between panels: the civilian panel is flat overcast, the flash panel is blown out, and the hero panel catches golden hour sun that wasn't present in the first frame, revealing the shots were filmed at different times. The 16mm stock shows different grain density in each panel — the flash panel's grain exploding in the overexposed center. The composite seams between panels show as thin vertical lines where the optical printer's mattes didn't perfectly align, a few frames of double-exposure visible as ghosting at the edges. The palette shifts across the triptych: civilian earth tones, flash white, hero primaries. The mood is the magic trick of tokusatsu — transformation as editing, the cut as superpower.

prompts.title: 80s — Villain Throne Room
prompts.subject: a performer
prompts.text: A wide shot of a villain's throne room set — the Toei studio aesthetic of maximalist evil on a minimal budget. A performer in an elaborate villain costume sits on a throne carved from painted Styrofoam, the throne's armrests sculpted into dragon heads whose teeth are individually glued plastic pieces, some slightly crooked. The villain's costume is the set's true centerpiece: a black and gold robe with rigid shoulder armor made from vacuum-formed plastic sheeting painted with automotive metallic lacquer, a high collar framing a mask that covers the upper face — the mask's surface showing the telltale ripple texture of a plaster mold, with eye holes that are slightly too large, revealing the performer's actual eye makeup (heavy black liner) and the foam latex edge where mask meets skin. Horns rise from the mask's temples — rigid fiberglass, one slightly longer than the other from a mold imperfection. The throne room set: walls painted in dark purple with silver lightning-bolt motifs stenciled on, columns made from cardboard tubes wrapped in metallic paper, a crystal ball on a stand (a bowling ball spray-painted silver, its finger holes visible from certain angles), and two background minion figures in black bodysuits and simple masks standing at rigid attention. The floor is painted black plywood showing crew footprints in the matte paint. Practical lighting from below — colored gels over floor-mounted work lights — casts dramatic uplight on the villain, creating sinister shadows in the mask's eye holes and revealing the spray-paint drips on the shoulder armor. Dry ice fog pours from behind the throne, pumped through a hidden tube. Shot on 16mm with the flat, slightly warm studio lighting of Toei's sound stages. The palette is villain-theatrical: black, gold, purple, silver, the red of hidden eye makeup, fog white. The mood is tokusatsu villainy — menace constructed from hardware store materials and performed with absolute theatrical commitment.

prompts.title: 70s — Mecha Launch Bay
prompts.subject: a young man
prompts.text: A medium shot inside a mecha launch bay — the set is a masterpiece of forced perspective: the bay walls converge toward a painted backdrop showing the open sky, creating the illusion of a vast hangar from a set that's actually twelve feet deep. A young man runs toward camera in a flight suit — orange polyester with white chest armor molded from vacuum-formed PETG, the armor showing the slight waviness of hand-formed plastic. He wears a helmet under his arm, his hair matted from a previous take's helmet wear, sweat running from his sideburn to his jaw. Behind him, the "mecha" — visible as a painted flat: a massive robot's legs painted on a wooden panel with remarkable detail, the perspective designed to appear three-dimensional from this specific camera angle but obviously flat if the camera moved two feet in either direction. The launch bay's walls are corrugated aluminum sheets with riveted seams, some rivets missing, the aluminum dented at waist height from crew traffic. Practical warning lights — repurposed car brake lights behind red lenses — flash in sequence along the wall, the sequence controlled by an off-camera crew member toggling relays, the timing slightly uneven. Steam jets from hidden nozzles cross the corridor at knee height, the steam catching the red warning lights and going pink. The floor is metal grating — genuine industrial grating — with cables running beneath. Shot on 16mm with the bay's mixed practical lighting: cool overhead fluorescents, warm red warning strobes, and the natural daylight leaking from the painted backdrop at the far end. The grain is heavy and warm, the fluorescents adding a slight green cast to his skin while the red strobes paint one side of his face in vivid color. The palette is launch-urgent: orange suit, white armor, red strobes, aluminum gray, steam pink. The mood is tokusatsu's industrial sublime — the mecha is a painting, the danger is real running.

prompts.title: 80s — Schoolgirl Monster Attack
prompts.subject: a young woman
prompts.text: A medium shot in a Tokyo street set — actually a Toei studio backlot dressed as a commercial district, the storefronts flat facades with real signage salvaged from demolished shops, some signs in genuine Japanese with others showing production-made approximations whose kanji is slightly wrong. A young woman in a school uniform — navy sailor fuku with a red neckerchief, white socks and brown loafers — runs directly toward camera with an expression of genuine alarm, her schoolbag clutched to her chest, her hair flying. Behind her, looming above the storefronts, a monster: a performer in a suit visible from the waist up above the false building tops, the creature a baroque amphibian thing with bulbous eyes made from modified swimming goggles coated in rubber, a mouth full of foam teeth — some broken from previous episodes, the stumps painted dark to simulate rot — and tentacle appendages made from pool noodles wrapped in painted latex that wave with a stiff, unconvincing menace as crew members off-screen manipulate the wires attached to each tentacle tip. A practical explosion fires at the base of a storefront — the balsa wood facade crumbling satisfyingly, a miniature car parked in front bouncing from the squib's blast, the pyrotechnic producing a vivid orange fireball with a black smoke cap that the 16mm stock renders with characteristic warmth. Debris — pre-broken chunks of plaster and balsa — rains down from an overhead release. The shot is undercranked to 20fps, making her running slightly too fast and the debris fall slightly too slow, creating the dreamlike physics specific to tokusatsu action. The palette is urban-attack: school navy, storefront colors, monster gray-green, explosion orange. The mood is tokusatsu's emotional core — genuine terror performed at a rubber monster, the schoolbag as the last symbol of normalcy in a world where pool-noodle tentacles are a legitimate threat.

prompts.title: 70s — Hero Sunset Cliff
prompts.subject: a figure
prompts.text: A wide shot at genuine golden hour — the one moment in a tokusatsu shooting schedule where nature provides the production value the budget cannot. A lone figure in a sentai suit — white with red trim, the spandex catching the golden light and going warm amber, the helmet's visor becoming a horizontal slash of reflected sunset — stands at the edge of a real cliff overlooking the Pacific, the ocean below churning with actual surf. The suit shows the day's wear: dust on the boots from quarry stunts, a grass stain on the left knee from a fall, a small tear at the elbow repaired with matching thread in slightly wrong tension. The figure stands in the classic tokusatsu hero pose: legs apart, fists clenched at the sides, cape — a rectangle of polyester satin attached at the shoulders with visible snap fasteners — billowing in the genuine ocean wind. The cape's hem is fraying, threads catching the backlight in fine golden lines. The setting is unaugmented reality — the cliff, the ocean, the sky — and the contrast between the obviously handmade costume and the authentic grandeur of the natural landscape creates the specific emotional frequency of tokusatsu at its best. Shot on 16mm Fuji — the golden hour light producing the stock's warmest possible rendering, the grain fine in the bright sky but heavy in the cliff shadows, the ocean a luminous plane of reflected gold. The wind is strong enough to make the cape's snap fasteners audible on set. The palette is heroic-natural: sunset gold, ocean blue, suit white warming to amber, cape satin catching fire. The mood is the image that every tokusatsu series builds toward — the hero alone against the sky, the suit ridiculous and the silhouette sincere.

prompts.title: 80s — Foam Monster Workshop
prompts.subject: a creature
prompts.text: A behind-the-scenes medium shot — the camera positioned inside the Tsuburaya Productions creature workshop, shooting a monster suit on a mannequin stand under flat fluorescent work lights. The suit is mid-construction: the foam latex body shell is complete — a chunky bipedal reptilian with exaggerated proportions, the foam still unpainted and showing its natural pale tan color with visible seam lines where the mold pieces were joined and the overflow trimmed with scissors. One arm is fully detailed with sculpted scales and painted claws, the other arm still bare foam awaiting its skin coat. The head sits separately on the workbench beside the body — its jaw mechanism exposed, a system of bicycle brake cables and small springs that will operate the mouth, the cables terminated with small handles that the suit performer will grip inside the chest cavity. Glass eyes — taxidermy supply, amber with vertical pupils — are set into the foam skull sockets with visible hot glue overflow. Paint pots and airbrush equipment surround the workbench: automotive paints in metallic greens and browns, reference photographs of lizards and deep-sea fish pinned to the wall, a hand-drawn diagram showing the cable routing for the jaw. A technician's coffee cup sits on the workbench beside the monster head, a lit cigarette balanced on the cup's rim, its smoke curling past the creature's unfinished face. Shot on 16mm — the flat fluorescent work lighting producing the slightly green-tinged, shadowless quality of an industrial workspace, the grain moderate, the foam's texture rendered with clinical detail. The palette is workshop-honest: foam tan, paint pot colors, fluorescent green-white, coffee brown, cigarette smoke. The mood is craftsmanship — the monster before it becomes a monster, still just foam and cables and someone's skilled hands.

prompts.title: 70s — Wire-Fu Rooftop Duel
prompts.subject: two figures
prompts.text: A wide shot on a rooftop set — a flat platform dressed with air conditioning units made from painted cardboard boxes and a water tower constructed from a modified oil drum. Two figures face each other in combat stances: the hero in a white martial arts gi modified with metallic trim and a flowing red sash, the villain in a black bodysuit with a cape and a skull-motif mask whose jawline doesn't quite match the performer's actual jaw, creating a gap visible at the chin. Both are attached to wire rigs — the wires visible as thin dark lines against the sky cyclorama backdrop, running upward to a steel-beam rig above the stage where crew members in black T-shirts are partially visible at the frame's extreme upper edge. The hero launches into a spinning kick — the wire rig lifting him slightly too high for the force of his jump, creating the characteristic floating quality of wire-fu, his gi flaring outward in a spiral that reveals the wire harness belt beneath, secured with a carabiner. The villain receives the kick — reacting a fraction before contact, the choreography's timing slightly off, creating the endearingly unconvincing impact that defines the genre. A practical spark effect fires from a squib on the villain's chest — a shower of titanium sparks spraying outward in a cone, some sparks visibly bouncing off the rooftop set and landing on the painted cardboard air conditioners. The kick's force sends the villain sliding backward — actually pulled by a separate wire at the waist — across the rooftop surface, which is painted plywood whose paint has scuffed away at the sliding mark from multiple takes. Shot on 16mm — the grain emphasized by the overcast sky cyclorama behind, the wires catching occasional glints, the spark effect overexposing into a bright orange streak. The palette is duel-classic: white gi, black bodysuit, red sash, titanium sparks, sky gray. The mood is the controlled chaos of tokusatsu fight choreography — every punch planned, every wire visible, every spark real, and the total commitment of the performers selling every impossible moment.

prompts.title: 80s — Base Explosion Escape
prompts.subject: two young adults
prompts.text: A wide shot of two young adults running through a corridor set as it "explodes" behind them — the corridor walls lined with pre-scored panels rigged with small pyrotechnic charges that fire in sequence, each charge blowing out a panel section in a shower of balsa fragments, sparks, and theatrical smoke. The male performer wears a military-style tactical uniform — khaki fabric with armored shoulder pads molded from foam, a holster belt with a chrome ray gun whose barrel is a modified flashlight housing. The female performer wears a fitted jumpsuit in white with blue trim — the jumpsuit's synthetic fabric catching each explosion's flash in brief specular pops. Both run at full speed, their expressions of alarm not entirely performed — the charges are real pyrotechnics, and the concussive pops are genuine. The corridor floor is littered with debris from previous takes: broken panel pieces, scattered sparks that have burned small marks into the painted surface, a fog machine hose visible at the baseboard pumping smoke that the performers run through. Ceiling tiles — lightweight foam panels — drop on cue from fishing-line releases, one tile bouncing off the male performer's shoulder pad with a visible flinch. The camera tracks backward ahead of them on a dolly — the dolly's wheels visible at the extreme bottom of frame, the tracking slightly unsteady. Shot on 16mm — each pyrotechnic flash overexposing the negative in a brief white burst that blooms through the surrounding frame, the smoke catching the light in orange-amber volumes, the grain heavy and dancing in the dark corridor sections between explosions. The palette is escape-chaos: khaki, white jumpsuit, orange explosions, gray smoke, corridor panel blue. The mood is tokusatsu action at its most physically real — the actors are literally running from actual small explosions, and the camera is running with them.

prompts.title: 70s — Alien Council Chamber
prompts.subject: five performers
prompts.text: A wide shot of an alien council chamber — five performers seated around a circular table on a raised platform, each wearing elaborate alien ruler costumes that represent the zenith of Toei's costume department's ambition and the nadir of their materials budget. The lead figure wears a robe of metallic gold fabric — a curtain material purchased in bulk, the lining visible where the robe gapes at the chest — with a crown that combines vacuum-formed plastic, Christmas ornaments, and what appears to be a modified chandelier piece, the whole construction wobbling slightly when the performer turns their head. Other council members sport similarly ambitious headpieces: one with a tall Egyptian-inspired headdress made from cardboard and metallic tape, another with organic horns sculpted from expanding foam painted in pearlescent automotive paint, a third with a full-face mask whose breathing holes are visible as two small circles beneath the painted-on nose. The table is a circle of plywood on a central pedestal, its surface covered in metallic contact paper that's bubbling at one edge. A "holographic display" at the table's center is a spinning plastic cylinder with a light bulb inside and colored gel filters, projecting colored light patterns on the council members' faces. The chamber walls: draped black fabric hiding the studio walls, with metallic stars glued to the drapes — some stars curling at the corners where the glue has dried. Dry ice fog crawls across the floor from a machine hidden behind the dais. Shot on 16mm under dramatic low-key lighting — colored gels on the key lights painting each council member in a different dominant hue, the grain heavy in the dark drapes, the metallic fabrics producing bright specular highlights. The palette is alien-regal: gold, purple, green, metallic silver, colored light, fog white. The mood is the grand delusion of tokusatsu world-building — a galactic parliament realized with curtain fabric and Christmas ornaments, performed with Shakespearean gravity.

prompts.title: 80s — Transformation Henshin
prompts.subject: a young man
prompts.text: A close-up sequence of a transformation device activation — the prop held at arm's length toward the camera by a young man whose face is set in fierce determination, the veins in his forearm visible from the grip. The transformation device is a wrist-mounted gadget — a modified digital watch housing with a chrome bezel, a large crystal center piece (a faceted acrylic bead from a craft supply store, catching the light beautifully despite its origin), and a small spring-loaded button that the performer presses with his thumb, the spring mechanism audible as a tiny click in the otherwise silent studio. His civilian outfit — a leather jacket over a T-shirt, jeans, sneakers — will be replaced in the next cut by a full sentai suit. His face in this extreme moment: jaw clenched, eyes wide with performed intensity, perspiration at the temples from repeated takes under the studio lights, the makeup minimal — just enough foundation to even his skin tone under the lights, the coverage ending visibly at his jawline. His hair is styled in the specific way of early-80s Japanese television heroes: slightly too long, slightly too perfect, held with product that the studio lights cause to gleam. Behind him, a practical colored-light effect: a crew member waves a colored gel in front of a focused lamp, creating moving colored light patterns across his face and the studio backdrop — the technique visible as shifting bands of color rather than the intended "energy aura." Shot on 16mm with a slightly telephoto lens that compresses his face and the transformation device into the same focal plane, the grain present and warm, the colored light effects adding vivid hue shifts that the Fuji stock renders with its characteristic warmth. The palette is henshin-charged: leather brown, device chrome, crystal refraction, colored gel sweep, determined skin warmth. The mood is the frozen instant before transformation — every tokusatsu hero's most human moment, the last frame of civilian identity before the cut to spandex.

prompts.title: 70s — Underwater Monster Lair
prompts.subject: a creature
prompts.text: A wide shot of an underwater lair set — achieved entirely dry, the "underwater" effect created by shooting through a glass tank of water placed between the camera and the set, the water's surface visible at the top of frame as a wobbling meniscus that distorts everything above it. The lair is a cave set: papier-mâché stalactites hanging from a wire grid, the cave walls molded from plaster over chicken wire with the wire occasionally poking through at the thinner sections, the floor scattered with real rocks supplemented by painted foam pieces that are distinguishable by their slightly too-uniform texture. In the center, a monster: a creature suit designed to read as aquatic — rubber fins attached to the forearms and calves, a head with gills made from layered foam pieces that flutter unconvincingly when the suit performer breathes, and bulbous eyes made from halved ping-pong balls painted with reflective automotive paint. The creature sits on a "coral throne" — Styrofoam carved with a hot wire and painted in vivid pinks and oranges, the hot-wire marks visible as smooth channels in the foam's texture. Practical lighting from below — work lights with blue and green gels placed on the cave floor — creates the aquatic atmosphere, the colored light reflecting off the water tank between camera and set, producing genuine caustic ripple patterns that dance across the cave walls and the monster suit. Air bubbles are added via a hidden aquarium pump in the water tank, rising through the frame and adding movement. Shot on 16mm — the water tank adding a layer of soft distortion and color shift over the already-grainy image, the blue-green gels pushing the Fuji stock's warm bias toward a teal compromise, grain visible in every shadow. The palette is undersea-practical: teal-blue, cave gray, coral pink-orange, monster rubber green, caustic light patterns. The mood is tokusatsu's most inventive technique — the tank-of-water trick creating a genuinely convincing underwater effect from dry studio materials.

prompts.title: 80s — Giant Robot Model Shot
prompts.subject: a robot figure
prompts.text: A low-angle wide shot of a giant robot model — approximately 60cm tall, constructed from painted styrene, resin, and die-cast metal components — photographed against a real sunset sky to sell the scale. The robot stands in a heroic pose on a miniature terrain base: a rocky hillside made from carved and painted insulation foam, with miniature trees (dried herbs and moss on wire armatures) and a tiny bridge (balsa and wire) in the foreground. The model's detail is extraordinary at this scale: panel lines scribed into the styrene with a hobby knife, tiny decals applied with microsurgical precision, weathering achieved with dry-brushed enamel paint and pin-washes of dark oil that settle into the panel lines. The joints show the limits of the medium: the elbow is a visible poly-cap joint, the waist a ball-and-socket whose socket housing is just barely concealed by a sculpted armor skirt. One fist is raised skyward, the other holds a miniature sword — a chrome-plated brass piece that catches the real sunset in a blinding specular flash. The real sky behind provides the production value that no studio backdrop could match: genuine clouds in amber and violet, the sun just below frame, backlighting the robot's silhouette with a warm rim that makes the styrene glow. The miniature terrain's forced perspective is nearly perfect from this angle — the tiny trees read as distant full-size trees against the sky. Shot on 35mm for this hero shot — the finer grain and wider latitude lending the model shot a cinematic quality distinct from the episode's 16mm coverage. The palette is sunset-heroic: sunset amber, robot white and blue, terrain green-brown, sky violet, chrome sword flare. The mood is tokusatsu's grandest illusion — a 60cm model that, for this one frame, against this one sky, becomes genuinely monumental.

prompts.title: 70s — Evil Footsoldier Army
prompts.subject: a group of performers
prompts.text: A wide shot of approximately twenty performers in matching black bodysuits and identical gray masks — the evil foot soldier army of a sentai villain, a staple of the genre. The bodysuits are cheap, thin, and slightly different shades of black — some blacker than others, revealing different fabric batches — with visible underwear lines on several performers. The masks are vacuum-formed from a single mold: smooth featureless faces with angular eye slits and a stylized grimace, each mask identical except for the slight warping differences inherent in hand-pulling plastic over a buck — some masks have a slightly crooked nose ridge, others a bubbled surface at the cheek. The army stands in a geometric formation — three rows of roughly seven — in a public park that the production has rented for the morning, genuine cherry blossom trees visible at the frame edges, a park bench that the art department forgot to remove partially visible behind the last row. Their poses are uniform: feet apart, arms crossed at the chest, chins raised — but the performers' varying heights and builds create an endearing irregularity in the formation. One performer in the back row is visibly shorter than the others, their mask sitting slightly too high on their face. The park's natural daylight provides flat, even illumination — no dramatic lighting, just the honest gray of an overcast Tokyo morning. Shot on 16mm — the grain giving the mass of identical masks a slight shimmer, the black bodysuits going slightly warm in the Fuji stock's rendering, the cherry blossoms registering as a soft pink wash at the edges. The palette is minion-uniform: black bodysuits, gray masks, park green, blossom pink, overcast sky. The mood is the disposable threat — twenty humans stripped of identity by a $3 vacuum-formed mask, an army assembled from stunt performers and acting students, standing in a public park with absolute menacing conviction.

prompts.title: 80s — Space Sheriff Armor
prompts.subject: a young man
prompts.text: A medium shot of a young man in mid-"metal hero" armor — the 80s tokusatsu evolution where chrome-finished suits replaced spandex. His armor is a full-body shell of vacuum-formed PET plastic coated in chrome automotive paint, the surface catching every light source in the studio with almost painful brightness — but at this angle, the chrome reveals its imperfections: orange-peel texture in the paint, a slight waviness in the vacuum-formed chest plate where the plastic didn't pull evenly over the buck, a visible seam at the shoulder where two halves of the pauldron are joined with internal rivets whose heads produce small bumps on the exterior. The helmet is the suit's masterpiece: a streamlined chrome shell with a blue visor and an elaborate crest — the crest is a separate fiberglass piece attached with two bolts visible at the base, the visor showing the performer's eyes behind it, blinking against the reflected studio lights. He stands in the hero pose — legs wide, arms slightly raised, fists clenched — the pose causing the armor to creak audibly where the PET plates overlap at the joints, the hip armor riding up slightly on the left side from repeated posing. The studio backdrop is a simple black drape, but the chrome armor reflects the studio itself: light stands, the camera operator, the edge of the set wall — the entire production crew ghosted across the hero's body in distorted funhouse reflection. Shot on 16mm — the chrome surface causing havoc with the exposure, the brightest reflections blooming into white while the suit's shadowed areas go dark and grainy, the grain dancing in the chrome's distorted reflections. The palette is chrome-hero: reflective silver, blue visor, black backdrop, the warm ghost of studio reflections, skin visible only at the chin and neck. The mood is tokusatsu's chrome evolution — the suit as mirror, reflecting everything including its own fabrication.

prompts.title: 70s — Monster Graveyard
prompts.subject: a young woman
prompts.text: A wide shot of a monster graveyard set — a surreal landscape where the suits of defeated monsters from previous episodes are partially buried in the ground, their foam-and-rubber bodies degrading into the set's artificial terrain. The set is a hellish diorama: a floor of painted hardboard with sculpted mounds representing a barren landscape, the sky a cyclorama painted in sickly yellow-green, the lighting from below with amber and red gels creating an infernal uplight. A young woman picks her way through the graveyard — she wears a torn civilian outfit, a school uniform with the jacket ripped and dirt-smeared, her hair tangled, a practical scrape on her cheek applied with makeup that's slightly too red to be convincing. She steps between the protruding monster remains: here a foam claw reaching from the ground, the paint flaking to reveal the pale foam beneath; there a mask half-buried, its single visible eye — a painted ping-pong ball — staring blankly upward, the rubber face sagging as the foam has degraded over months in storage. One complete monster torso leans against a rock formation, the zipper running up its back completely visible, the suit deflated without a performer inside, looking like a discarded skin. The practical lighting — work lights with colored gels on the ground — creates dramatic shadows that turn the recycled monster parts into genuinely unsettling sculptural forms. Dry ice fog crawls along the ground, pooling in the depressions, partially concealing the set's edges. Shot on 16mm with the colored practicals as the only light source — the grain heavy, the gel colors saturating the Fuji stock into vivid, unrealistic tones, the fog adding a soft diffusion layer. The palette is afterlife-lurid: amber, red, yellow-green sky, foam gray, degraded paint. The mood is tokusatsu's strangest poetry — the monsters after the story is done, their suits decaying into art, the schoolgirl walking through television's material unconscious.

prompts.title: 80s — Bike Chase Undercrank
prompts.subject: a figure
prompts.text: A tracking wide shot from a camera car — the camera mounted on the hood of a following vehicle, shooting forward at a motorcycle ridden by a figure in a full sentai suit. The motorcycle is a modified Honda CB with custom fiberglass bodywork in matching red — the bodywork's attachment brackets visible where the panels meet the frame, a chrome exhaust pipe that's been painted red but the paint has burned off near the header, returning to chrome. The rider's red spandex suit billows in the wind, the fabric vibrating at high frequency, the helmet's visor catching the road's surface in a reflected blur. The shot is undercranked to 20fps and projected at 24fps, making the motorcycle appear to move approximately 20% faster than its actual speed — the acceleration visible as a subtle dreamlike smoothness in the motion that isn't quite natural. The road is a real two-lane highway in rural Japan — rice paddies on both sides, telephone poles rhythmically passing, a mountain range in the blue distance. No traffic — the production has a police escort blocking the road, the escort vehicle's roof lights just visible at the extreme left edge of frame. The camera car's shadow stretches forward on the asphalt, occasionally touching the motorcycle's rear wheel. Shot on 16mm — the movement, undercranking, and camera vibration from the car creating a complex grain pattern where the grain seems to travel with the motion, the Fuji stock rendering the rural Japanese green with characteristic warmth, the motorcycle's red slightly bleeding into orange from the stock's response. Road surface texture streams past in detailed blur at the frame bottom. The palette is pursuit-primary: motorcycle red, asphalt gray, rice-paddy green, mountain blue, warm speed blur. The mood is tokusatsu in motion — practical speed, practical wind, the undercranking turning a 50km/h ride into something that feels heroically fast.

prompts.title: 70s — Scientist Lab Warning
prompts.subject: a young man
prompts.text: A medium shot in a scientist's laboratory set — the tokusatsu version of science: a desk covered in beakers (filled with colored water), a oscilloscope showing a repeated waveform (the prop department's own oscilloscope, borrowed and returned between episodes), a computer terminal made from a modified television set displaying scrolling green text (a card with printed text being slowly pulled past the screen by a crew member beneath the desk). A young man in a white lab coat — the coat a size too large, the sleeves rolled up to reveal his watch, a pen collection in the breast pocket that includes a prop "communicator" whose antenna extends — stares at a large wall-mounted screen showing a monster approaching a city, the footage being a rear-projection of miniature destruction footage from earlier in the episode, the rear-projection hotspot visible as a bright center with darkening edges. His face registers alarm with the specific performance style of 70s tokusatsu — broad, theatrical, the eyes widening beyond natural range, one hand raised in a gesture of warning, the other gripping the edge of the desk hard enough to shift one of the beakers. His skin under the flat fluorescent set lighting shows visible pores and the slight shadow of a five-o'clock shadow that the morning's shave couldn't fully address. Behind him on the wall: charts with Japanese text and technical diagrams that are actually modified anatomy posters with the labels replaced, a clock showing the wrong time, and a fire extinguisher that's a genuine safety requirement rather than a prop. Shot on 16mm — flat studio lighting, minimal grain in the well-lit lab, the rear-projection screen showing its own denser grain from the projected 16mm footage, the two layers of grain creating a visible texture difference between the "live" lab and the "projected" monster footage. The palette is science-functional: white coat, colored beaker water, green terminal text, rear-projection warm tones, fluorescent flat. The mood is the tokusatsu scientist — always aware of the monster before anyone else, always unbelieved, always right.

prompts.title: 80s — Sentai Roll Call
prompts.subject: five figures
prompts.text: A medium shot of five sentai heroes lined up in a row, executing their individual poses in sequence for the team roll call — the signature scene of every super sentai episode, performed here on an outdoor location: a concrete dam whose curved surface provides a dramatic architectural backdrop. Each performer in their colored suit — red, blue, yellow, pink, green — strikes a unique pose that's been rehearsed to mechanical precision: Red with feet wide and arms in an X-cross, Blue in a crane stance with one leg raised, Yellow in a low crouch with one fist forward, Pink in a gymnastics-inspired back arch, Green in a power stance with both fists at hip height. The poses are held for the camera — the performers' visible effort showing in the slight tremor of held positions, one performer's boot sliding fractionally on the damp concrete. Behind them, a practical pyrotechnic charge fires on cue — a line of five smoke pots in their respective colors, producing colored smoke columns that rise behind each hero in a matching palette. The smoke is gorgeous against the concrete dam — vivid primary colors mixing at the edges, catching the late afternoon sun. Two of the smoke pots produce slightly less volume than the others, the green one sputtering. The performers' suits show the day's work: dust on every boot, a grass stain on Yellow's elbow, a small tear at Blue's shoulder seam hastily repaired with thread that's slightly too dark. Shot on 16mm — the colored smoke overexposing slightly in the areas where it's densest, the concrete dam providing a neutral backdrop that makes the suits and smoke the only color. The Fuji stock loves these primaries — each suit saturated to its maximum while maintaining separation. The palette is roll-call-classic: five primary suits, five matching smoke columns, concrete gray, afternoon gold. The mood is the weekly ritual — five people in spandex on a dam, absolutely certain that their pose alone can defeat evil.

prompts.title: 70s — Cave Base Interior
prompts.subject: a group
prompts.text: A wide shot of the hero team's secret base — a cave set whose walls are sculpted from chicken-wire and plaster, the plaster showing a few stress cracks from the set's semi-permanent installation in the studio, the rock texture created by pressing real rocks into the wet plaster as stamps, each impression slightly too regular to be natural. In the center, a command console: a curved desk constructed from plywood and faced with brushed aluminum sheet metal, the surface studded with repurposed electronics — actual oscilloscope screens showing waveforms, military-surplus toggle switches with satisfying mechanical action, a row of colored indicator lights that are Christmas-tree bulbs behind colored plastic caps, one cap missing and showing the bare white bulb. Three team members in civilian clothes — 70s casual: wide-collar shirts, flared jeans, platform shoes — cluster around the console studying a wall-mounted display (a rear-projection screen showing a map graphic, the projector's fan noise implied by its warm glow at the screen's center). A fourth member sits at the console operating controls, a pair of headphones around their neck — the headphones are standard studio monitors, the coiled cable trailing to a junction box that's been painted silver to look technological. The cave walls are dressed with additional equipment: banks of reel-to-reel tape machines (genuine, borrowed from a radio station, their reels spinning with actual magnetic tape), blinking light panels that are perforated aluminum sheets with bulbs behind, and a large emblem of the team's logo mounted on the wall — painted on a wooden circle with slight drip marks in the enamel visible at close range. Shot on 16mm with the cave's mixed practical lighting: blue-gelled work lights along the base of the walls creating the "high-tech cave" ambiance, warm amber practicals at the console, the rear-projection adding its own warm cast. The grain is present throughout, the dark cave walls showing heavy noise, the lit console area relatively clean. The palette is base-functional: cave gray, aluminum silver, console amber, blue ambient, civilian earth tones. The mood is tokusatsu's domestic headquarters — the cave where adults in flared jeans save the world between episodes, using Christmas lights and borrowed oscilloscopes.

prompts.title: 80s — Kaiju Eye Detail
prompts.subject: a creature eye
prompts.text: An extreme close-up of a kaiju suit's eye — filling the entire frame, shot with a macro lens that reveals every detail of the prop's construction with forensic intimacy. The eye is approximately 15 centimeters in diameter: a hemisphere of clear resin cast over a hand-painted iris — the iris painted on a flat disc beneath the resin dome, showing individual brushstrokes in the radial pattern of amber, gold, and black, each stroke visible as a tiny ridge in the paint. The pupil is a void of pure black acrylic paint, its edge slightly irregular where the painter's hand wavered. The resin dome has a genuine optical quality — it catches the studio lights in a realistic specular highlight that sits on the surface and moves with the camera angle, giving the impression of a wet, living eye. Tiny air bubbles trapped in the resin during casting are visible as bright points within the dome, like miniature stars frozen in amber. The eye socket: foam latex sculpted and painted to suggest scaled skin, the paint job — airbrushed in layers of green, brown, and yellow — showing the overspray pattern at the edges where masking tape wasn't perfectly placed. The foam's surface texture at this magnification reveals the cell structure of the material — tiny open cells that catch light differently from the painted surface. A single practical tear effect — a glycerin drop — sits at the inner corner of the eye, catching the macro lens's ring light in a perfect specular crescent. Shot on 16mm with a +4 diopter — the extreme magnification reducing the depth of field to millimeters, the grain at this scale becoming a visible texture layer over the prop's surface, each silver halide cluster the size of one of the iris's painted brush strokes. The palette is biological-intimate: amber iris, black pupil, foam-green socket, glycerin-clear tear, resin dome catching light. The mood is tokusatsu seen closer than it was ever designed to be seen — and somehow, at this scale, the craft becomes more impressive, not less.

prompts.title: 70s — Miniature Tank Battle
prompts.subject: miniature vehicles
prompts.text: A wide shot of a miniature battlefield — 1:24 scale model tanks rolling across a terrain board of sculpted plaster over chicken wire, painted in earth tones with scattered model-railroad grass and tiny trees made from twisted wire and lichen. The tanks are modified plastic model kits — approximately 15cm long — with added detail: antenna wire from guitar strings, fuel drums from wooden dowels, and hand-painted markings that are slightly too large for the scale. They roll on hidden tracks beneath the terrain surface, pulled by fishing line, their movement stuttering slightly as the line catches on a terrain irregularity. Between them, pyrotechnic charges embedded in the plaster explode in sequence — tiny orange fireballs with black smoke caps that are perfectly scaled, each explosion throwing up painted plaster debris that arcs convincingly through the air before landing in craters left by previous takes. One tank is rigged to be destroyed: a balsa-wood shell over a compressed-air charge that, when detonated, blows the tank's turret upward on a visible wire while the body shatters outward in a cascade of painted splinters. The camera is positioned at ground level within the miniature set — a lens hood buried in fake terrain, so the perspective places the viewer inside the battlefield. The destruction is photographed at 96fps for slow-motion playback, making the explosions billow with an eerily convincing weight. Shot on 16mm — the grain adding texture to the smoke, the pyrotechnic flashes overexposing in the high-speed footage, the earth tones of the terrain rendered with the warm Fuji bias. The palette is battle-terrain: earth brown, tank olive, explosion orange, smoke black-gray, plaster debris white. The mood is miniature warfare — every explosion hand-charged, every tank hand-built, destruction as craft.

prompts.title: 80s — Power Rangers Gymnasium
prompts.subject: a group of young adults
prompts.text: A medium wide shot of a high school gymnasium set — a sentai team in civilian identity, practicing martial arts in matching track suits of different colors (each matching their sentai suit color: red, blue, yellow, pink, black) on a genuine gymnasium floor whose varnish is scuffed and marked with game court lines. Five young adults perform synchronized kata — the choreography precise but their individual skill levels visibly different: the Red performer is clearly a trained martial artist with sharp, snapping movements; the Pink performer has gymnastics training visible in their flexibility but less power; the Blue performer is slightly behind the timing on every third move. Their track suits: cheap synthetic fabric with screen-printed team logos on the back, the printing slightly off-register on the Yellow suit, the fabric already pilling at the cuffs. The gymnasium behind them is real — not a set, an actual school gym rented for the day, with basketball hoops at each end, wooden bleachers folded against the wall, fluorescent tube lighting in wire-cage fixtures overhead. Through the high windows, actual daylight — the time pressure of a one-day location shoot visible in the crew's equipment shadows at the gym's far end. A boom microphone is visible at the extreme top of frame, hastily pulled up but not quite cleared. Shot on 16mm — the gymnasium's fluorescents creating the slightly green-tinged flat lighting of institutional spaces, the grain moderate, the track suit colors slightly muted by the fluorescent color temperature. The palette is civilian-sentai: five track suit colors, gym wood, fluorescent flat, daylight through windows. The mood is the secret identity — five heroes disguised as teenagers, their combat training hidden in plain sight as after-school exercise.

prompts.title: 70s — Giant Hero vs Building
prompts.subject: a giant figure
prompts.text: A wide shot framing the climactic moment of a giant hero's fight — the hero (a performer in a silver-and-red suit, approximately human-height) grapples with a monster (a performer in a green rubber suit with fin-like protrusions) against a backdrop of miniature buildings at approximately 1:50 scale. The hero's foot steps on a miniature office building — the balsa structure crumpling satisfyingly, tiny furniture pieces tumbling from the windows (visible as the small carved blocks they are), the building's facade splitting along pre-scored lines that allow it to collapse in a controlled pattern rather than randomly. The monster staggers backward from a blow — the performer's retreat constrained by the suit's leg mobility, creating the characteristic slow, heavy backward stumble of tokusatsu giants — and collides with a miniature radio tower (a wire construction with painted balsa cross-members) that bends and falls with a sparking practical effect at the base, the sparks produced by a steel-wool pad connected to a battery hidden in the tower's foundation. Between them on the miniature city street, tiny model cars — die-cast toys repainted in realistic colors — bounce from the vibration of the performers' movements. One car topples from a miniature bridge whose railing has already been dented from earlier in the scene. The sky is a blue cyclorama with cotton-ball clouds glued in place — one cloud slightly drooping from its adhesive losing grip under the studio lights. Shot on 16mm, undercranked to 20fps for slow-motion playback at 24fps — the slight speed reduction giving the destruction a weight and momentum that sells the scale, each fragment of balsa falling just slowly enough to read as concrete. The grain churns in the smoke from the sparking tower. The palette is city-destruction: silver hero, green monster, building gray-beige, fire orange, cyclorama blue. The mood is tokusatsu's weekly apocalypse — a city destroyed by Tuesday, rebuilt by Thursday, the balsa dust settling on the studio floor.

prompts.title: 80s — Cockpit Shaking Effect
prompts.subject: two young adults
prompts.text: A medium shot inside a spacecraft cockpit set — two young adults strapped into seats that are bolted to a platform being rocked by four crew members just out of frame, each gripping a corner of the platform and shaking it with slightly different rhythm, creating a complex, irregular vibration that's far more convincing than a mechanical shaker. The two performers — a man in a blue flight suit and a woman in a white one, both suits with matching insignia patches that are iron-on transfers slightly peeling at the edges — grip their seat armrests and perform the universal tokusatsu "being shaken" acting: heads whipping side to side in exaggerated motion, bodies lurching against the seat harnesses, the man's visor (pushed up on his helmet) bouncing down with each shake and being pushed back up between lurches. Sparks fly from a console panel — a practical effect achieved by a crew member behind the console striking a flint wheel from a cigarette lighter against a steel plate, producing a shower of orange sparks that arc outward convincingly. One overhead panel drops on a hinge — pre-rigged to fall at this moment — swinging down and dangling by its cable, the cable's attachment point visible as a drilled hole in the panel's edge. Smoke pours from the same console — a hidden smoke machine pumping theatrical haze through a hole cut in the console's back panel, the haze catching the sparks in vivid orange streaks. Shot on 16mm — the physical shaking of the platform translating to the camera as genuine camera shake, the grain dancing with the movement, the sparks overexposing into bright orange streaks against the darker cockpit interior. The palette is crisis-cockpit: blue and white suits, console gray, spark orange, smoke, warning-light red. The mood is tokusatsu's most honestly physical effect — the shaking is real, the sparks are real fire, the actors' alarm is half-performed and half-genuine.

prompts.title: 70s — Alien Planet Cyclorama
prompts.subject: a young woman
prompts.text: A wide shot of an alien planet surface set — a studio stage transformed into an extraterrestrial landscape through the specific craft vocabulary of 70s Japanese television production. The ground is a combination of real sand (trucked into the studio) and sculpted foam rocks painted in unrealistic but beautiful colors — deep purples and iridescent blues that no terrestrial geology would produce, the paint showing brush-direction marks. The sky is a large cyclorama painted in a gradient from blood red at the horizon to deep violet at the zenith, the canvas's weave texture visible in the raking studio light, the transition between colors showing the painter's blending strokes. Two "alien moons" hang from invisible wires above the cyclorama — spheres of papier-mâché painted in pearlescent white, their surfaces showing the newspaper texture beneath the paint where the papier-mâché wasn't sanded smooth. A young woman stands in this landscape wearing a flowing silver cape over a white bodysuit, the cape's cheap polyester satin catching the studio lights in a flat, characteristic way, the bodysuit showing a visible panty line and the outline of the performer's knee pads worn for earlier stunt work. Her hair is styled in an elaborate updo with metallic accessories — bobby pins painted silver. She stares into the middle distance with the specific expression of tokusatsu wonder: lips slightly parted, eyes wide, one hand raised toward one of the papier-mâché moons. The set is lit with dramatic colored gels — red from below matching the red horizon, a blue fill from above creating a split color temperature on her face. Dry ice fog crawls across the sand floor. Shot on 16mm — the colored lighting pushing the Fuji stock into vivid but slightly muddy saturation, the grain heavy in the dark violet sky areas, the fog adding soft diffusion. The palette is alien-painted: purple rock, red-violet sky, silver cape, white moon spheres, colored gel light. The mood is tokusatsu world-building at its most painterly — an alien planet constructed from sand, foam, and imagination.

prompts.title: 80s — Monster Suit Interior POV
prompts.subject: a performer
prompts.text: A unique POV shot from inside a monster suit — the camera lens positioned behind the creature's eye holes, shooting outward through the rubber mask's apertures. The view is restricted: two roughly circular openings showing the studio beyond in a binocular-like frame, the edges of the mask visible as out-of-focus dark rubber borders with the foam's cell structure visible at close range. Through the eye holes, the miniature city set is visible — tiny buildings, a painted sky backdrop, crew members adjusting pyrotechnic charges in the far background. The suit's interior is dimly visible at the frame edges: the inside of the foam latex skull showing brush marks from the adhesive that holds the outer skin to the underlying structure, a small battery pack for the jaw mechanism taped to the interior with gaffer tape, a strip of absorbent cloth at the forehead — a crude sweat band to keep perspiration from the performer's eyes. The performer's actual breathing is implied by the slight fogging of the eye holes, the condensation forming and clearing in a rhythm. Through the right eye hole, a crew member approaches with a spray bottle — misting the suit's exterior between takes to maintain the "wet creature" look. Through the left, the hero figure in their sentai suit waits at their mark, stretching their shoulders and rolling their neck — the human moments between takes. The limited field of view creates genuine claustrophobia. Shot on 16mm — the already-present grain amplified by the low light inside the suit, the exterior world visible through the eye holes overexposing slightly against the dark interior. The palette is interior-exterior: dark rubber interior, bright studio exterior, foam tan, the warm smudge of the performer's breath. The mood is the performer's secret experience — tokusatsu from the inside, where the monster is just a hot rubber room with two small windows to the world.

prompts.title: 70s — River Bank Ambush
prompts.subject: a group
prompts.text: A wide shot at a genuine river location — a rocky bank beside shallow rapids, the water real and cold, the performers' discomfort authentic. The hero team — three figures in matching blue jumpsuits — is ambushed by a squad of footsoldiers in black bodysuits and gray masks who emerge from behind the riverside boulders. The fight choreography is performed on the actual riverbank: rocky, uneven, slippery — one footsoldier visibly stumbles on a wet rock before recovering into a combat stance, the stumble incorporated rather than re-shot. Kicks splash in the shallow water — real spray catching the backlight in crystal arcs. One hero performs a shoulder throw on a footsoldier — the stunt performer hitting the rocky shore with a visible impact, the fall pad concealed beneath a thin layer of river pebbles that scatters on impact. A practical smoke bomb — a military-surplus colored smoke grenade in red — has been deployed upstream, its vivid red smoke drifting across the scene and mixing with the natural river mist, creating an atmospheric haze that the 16mm stock renders with characteristic warmth. The natural environment provides everything the studio cannot: real water texture, genuine atmospheric haze, the sound-implied rush of rapids, actual cold making the performers' breath visible. The camera position is across the river, shooting with a moderate telephoto that compresses the fighters against the rising bank. Shot on 16mm Fuji — the grain moderate in the daylight, the water reflections producing dancing highlights, the red smoke saturating beautifully against the natural greens. The palette is location-natural: river blue-gray, rocky brown, jumpsuit blue, footsoldier black, smoke red, forest green. The mood is tokusatsu on location — where the choreography meets actual physics, and the river doesn't care about the shooting schedule.

prompts.title: 80s — Combining Robot Sequence
prompts.subject: robot models
prompts.text: A composited sequence shot — five separate model vehicles photographed individually against black velvet, then optically combined in post to create the illusion of a combining robot transformation. Each vehicle is a hand-built model approximately 30cm long: a jet fighter, a tank, a submarine, a drill vehicle, and a command car — each constructed from styrene sheet, filled with lead shot for weight, and painted in matching red-and-white livery with hand-applied decals. The combination happens in freeze-frames connected by zoom-blur transitions: the jet folds its wings (stop-motion, the wings repositioned by hand between frames, 24 incremental adjustments creating approximately one second of animated screen time), the tank's turret rotates to become an arm (a gear mechanism inside the model, operated by a key wound between frames), the drill vehicle extends its drill bit upward to form the other arm. The optical combination is visible in its execution: the black velvet backgrounds don't perfectly match in density between the separately filmed elements, creating subtle brightness differences where the models overlap. Matting edges show — a thin dark line around each vehicle where the rotoscoped matte doesn't perfectly follow the model's edge, the line thicker at complex geometry like the jet's tail fins. The zoom-blur transitions are optical printer work — the image zooming into the film grain itself, the grain pattern enlarging to abstract blocks of color before resolving into the next configuration. Shot on 35mm for the model work — the finer grain and better color providing the hero-shot quality that separates combination sequences from the regular 16mm episode footage. The palette is combination-primary: red-white vehicle livery, black velvet, zoom-blur color streaks, the warm amber of the optical printer's light source. The mood is tokusatsu's most elaborate illusion — five models becoming one robot through patience, craft, and the optical printer's transformative power.

prompts.title: 70s — Female Commander Bridge
prompts.subject: a young woman
prompts.text: A medium close-up of a young woman seated in the commander's chair of a spacecraft bridge set — a high-backed swivel chair upholstered in red vinyl that squeaks when she shifts weight, the chair mounted on a raised platform so that she towers above the crew stations arranged in a semicircle below. She wears a uniform jacket in deep blue with metallic gold frogging across the chest — the frogging is actually gold-painted cord glued to the jacket, a few spots of glue visible where the cord wasn't pressed firmly enough. Matching blue trousers tucked into knee-high boots that are clearly modified riding boots, their equestrian buckles painted gold. Her hair is styled in a severe updo with a hairpiece adding volume — the hairpiece's slightly different texture and color visible where it meets her natural hair. Her expression is one of command: eyes narrowed, jaw set, one hand gripping the chair's armrest, the other raised with index finger extended in a decisive gesture. The crew stations below her show their budget-constrained details: a communications console made from a repurposed audio mixing board with relabeled sliders, a navigation station whose star chart is a photograph backlit from behind the panel, the photograph's edges curling slightly from the heat. Screen-accurate details: a steaming cup of tea on a crew member's console, a clipboard with actual Japanese script. Shot on 16mm with dramatic low lighting — a strong key from above the commander's chair creating a pool of authority light, the crew stations below lit by their own console practicals. The grain is moderate, the deep blue uniform going slightly warm in the Fuji rendering. The palette is bridge-authority: deep blue, gold frogging, red vinyl, console amber, warm skin in dramatic light. The mood is 70s tokusatsu's quiet feminism — a woman in the commander's chair, the modified riding boots planted firmly on the platform, the glued-on frogging worn with genuine authority.

prompts.title: 80s — City Miniature Night Attack
prompts.subject: a monster figure
prompts.text: A wide shot of a nighttime miniature city set — the same 1:25 scale construction methodology but now lit for night, which transforms the cheap materials into something genuinely atmospheric. The miniature buildings have working interior lights — tiny grain-of-wheat bulbs wired in parallel, some flickering from loose connections, their warm amber glow spilling through the clear-plastic windows and casting tiny pools on the miniature streets. Miniature streetlights — LED bulbs on wire poles — line the streets in receding rows, their light creating a convincing sense of scale and depth. The sky backdrop is unlit, reading as pure black. Into this miniature nightscape, a monster enters from frame left — a performer's legs in a creature suit visible from the waist down, the suit's rubber feet crushing a miniature sedan whose headlights were wired live and now flash once as the car crumbles, the bulb popping with a visible spark. The monster's other foot lands on a miniature gas station — a detailed model with a tiny canopy and hand-painted signage — triggering a pyrotechnic charge that produces an orange fireball perfectly scaled to the surroundings, the explosion's light reflecting in every miniature window on the street, casting monster-leg shadows across building facades. Tiny miniature fire effects — cotton balls soaked in lighter fluid and ignited — burn in the wreckage, adding flickering practical light to the scene. The miniature city at night is genuinely beautiful — the warm window lights, the streetlight rows, the fire — and the monster destroying it is genuinely menacing in silhouette. Shot on 16mm — the dark set requiring wide-open aperture, the grain heavy and atmospheric, the tiny practicals blooming slightly in the fast stock. The palette is night-destruction: warm window amber, streetlight white, explosion orange, fire flicker, monster silhouette black against it all. The mood is tokusatsu's nocturnal masterpiece — when the lights are real and the destruction is fire-lit, the miniatures transcend their materials.

prompts.title: 70s — Hostage Warehouse
prompts.subject: a young woman
prompts.text: A medium shot in a warehouse set — corrugated metal walls, concrete floor, a single bare bulb hanging from a chain providing harsh, swinging practical light that causes shadows to move rhythmically across the scene. A young woman is tied to a metal chair — the rope work obvious movie rope: thick, white, wrapped decoratively rather than functionally, loose enough that she could extract her hands if the script required it immediately. She wears a torn blouse and a skirt showing a practical rip at the hem — the tear too clean to be genuine, the costume department having cut it with scissors along the fabric's grain. Her face shows makeup-applied distress: smudged mascara tracks on her cheeks (glycerin-based, staying wet under the lights), a practical bruise on her jaw (stipple sponge application, the purple slightly too uniform), and her hair pulled loose from its style in an artful dishevelment that maintains its screen appeal. Despite the victim scenario, her expression holds defiance — jaw thrust forward, eyes blazing at an off-screen captor, the performance carrying more conviction than the production design.
